items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the real property actions and proceedings law, in relation to
establishing the uniform partition of heirs property act
items.lawSection: Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4865

SPONSOR: HOYLMAN
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the real property actions and
proceedings law, in relation to establishing the uniform partition of
heirs property act

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill amends the Real Property Actions and Proceedings
Law by adding a new section 993 entitled the Uniform Partition of Heirs
Property Act.

-Subdivision 1 of section 993 establishes the short title of the
section.

-Subdivision 2 of section 993 defines the terms used throughout the Act,
including "heirs property," defined as real property held in tenancy in
common in which there is no agreement in a record binding all of the
cotenants which governs the partition of the property, one or more of
the cotenants acquired title from a relative, and either at least 20% of
the interests in the property are held by co-tenants who are relatives,
at least 20% of the interests in the property are held by individuals
who acquired title from a relative, or at least 20% or more of the
co-tenants are relatives.

-Subdivision 3 of section 993 applies the provisions of this section to
partition actions filed on or after the effective date of the law and
specifies that this section supplements existing New York State law
governing partitions, except where the provisions of existing law are
inconsistent with this section, in which case the requirements of the
Act apply.

-Subdivision 4 of section 993 establishes that the Act shall not limit
or affect the existing method by which service of a complaint in a
partition action made be made, as well as establishing the procedures if
a plaintiff in a partition action seeks an order of notice by publica-
tion.

-Subdivision 5 of section 993 requires any court-designated commission-
ers to be disinterested, impartial, and not a party to or a participant
in the partition action.

-Subdivision 6 of section 993 requires courts to determine the fair
market value of heirs property that is the subject of a partition
action, and establishes procedures for court-ordered appraisals.

-Subdivision 7 of section 993 gives co-tenants the right of first
refusal to purchase the interests of the co-tenant or co-tenants that
are seeking a partition by sale, based on the proportionate share of the
fair market value of the property, and establishes related procedures.

-Subdivision 8 of section 993 establishes that, if no co-tenant exer-
cises their right to buy out a co-tenant seeking a partition by sale,
the court shall first consider ordering a partition in kind, unless the
court determines that a partition in kind will result in great manifest
prejudice to the co-tenants as a group, in which case a partition by
sale will be ordered.

-Subdivision 9 of section 993 establishes the considerations a court
must make in determining whether to order partition in kind.

-Subdivision 10 of section 993 requires that a court-ordered sale of
heirs property to be an open-market sale unless the court finds that a
sale by sealed bid or auction would be in the best interest of the
co-tenants, and establishes related procedures, including the appoint-
ment of a real estate broker.

-Subdivision 11 of section 993 requires the appointed real estate broker
to file a report with the court within seven days of receiving an offer
to purchase the property.

Section 2 of the bill is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

As a general rule under current New York law, when real property has
multiple owners who hold the property as tenants in common, any one
co-owner can try to force the sale of the property by filing a partition
action in court under Article 9 of the Real Property Actions and
Proceedings Law.

In recent years, predatory real estate speculators have taken advantage
of New York's laws governing partition actions by purchasing a stake in
a residential property - usually after a number of family members have
inherited the property - and then using that owners hip stake to file a
partition action to dispossess the family of the property through a
forced sale, often for pennies on the dollar relative to the actual
value of the property. Lower- and middle-class families are particularly
susceptible to these types of schemes, as they often do not engage in
the kind of sophisticated estate planning that could prevent predatory
partitioning actions.

This legislation would address the issue of predatory partition actions,
while preserving a co-owner's right to sell his or her share of the
property. The Act would only apply in situations where at least one of
the co-owners has inherited their property interest from a relative and
there is no written agreement otherwise governing partition among the
owners. In such situations, there are a number of protections in place
when a co-owner files for a partition order:

-The co-owner requesting the partition must give notice to all of the
other co-owners.

-The court must order an independent appraisal to determine the proper-
ty's fair market value.

-Any co-owner may exercise a right of first refusal to buy out the
interest of the co-owner seeking partition for a proportional share of
the court-determined fair market value.

-If no co-owner elects to buy out the co-owner seeking partition, the
court must first consider ordering a partition-in-kind if the property
can be physically divided.

-If a partition-in-kind would be inappropriate, and the court orders a
partition-by-sale, the property must be offered for sale on the open
market at a price no lower than the court-determined value for a reason-
able period of time and in a commercially reasonable manner.

As of March 2019, eleven other states and the U.S. Virgin Islands have
adopted similar legislation.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
